title: What is known about 1RB0LE_1LC0RA_1RD0RC_1LA0LD_1LB0LF_1LC---
description: Proof status of the six-state BB(6) holdout 1RB0LE_1LC0RA_1RD0RC_1LA0LD_1LB0LF_1LC---.
intro: Nobody knows whether this six-state, two-symbol Turing machine halts when started on a blank tape: it is one of the holdouts left open by the bbchallenge project. This page lists what has been established about it, sorted by what each result rests on.
verdict: The question is open. Lean proves two erasing runs and the situations that lead to a halt (kernel), and no halt in the first 107 steps (native_decide); the C simulator finds no halt in 109 steps.

What it does. At the left end the tape is a mix of runs of the word 001011 and short blocks like 000 10 11 0 11 0 11; at the right end it is stretches of 1010… separated by 00. The sweeps translate between the two; C erases blocks of 1s going right and D erases them going left. The mixture changes without visible order.
Where a halt would come from. Only F reading a 1 halts; F is entered from E reading a 1, so 1 E>1 halts. F itself is rare (111 thousand visits in 2·108 steps), always on a 0.

claims.title: The halting configurations
claims.text: The machine stops exactly when it reads the symbol of a halting transition (F1); the generated statement covers every configuration.

claims.title: Where a halt can come from
claims.text: If the machine halts on its third step from a configuration, that configuration is one of: A with 1 two left, 1 left, 1 under the head. So a run can reach a halt only through one of these patterns, and a proof that the machine never halts only has to rule them out. The proof splits on the state and the five cells around the head.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10,000 steps
claims.text: The list simulator of the shared library, proved to agree with the machine's semantics, runs 10,000 steps from blank tape without a halt, evaluated by Lean's kernel.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps
claims.text: The same run, evaluated by compiled code.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>9</sup> steps
claims.text: The C simulator tools/c/triage.c runs 109 steps without a halt; at the end 22,985 cells have been visited and 11,860 of them hold a 1.

claims.title: Growth shape: sqrt/sqrt
claims.text: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.501). Right of the start it grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.476).

claims.title: Shift rules
claims.text: C erases any block of 1s going right, one step a cell; D with a 1 ahead erases any block of 1s going left.

claims.title: The halting situations
claims.text: 1 E>1 halts after one step, 1 1 A>1 after two, 1 1 1 D>0 after three, 1 1 C>0 0 after four.

claims.title: F never reads a 1 in 2·10<sup>8</sup> steps
claims.text: In the first 2·10<sup>8</sup> steps the machine is in state F 111,044 times, every time on a 0: the halting transition F1 is never close to firing in a way the run shows.

claims.title: Does it halt from blank tape?
claims.text: Not known. NGramCPS with n ≤ 10 and window CTL with K ≤ 7 leave it open.

explainer.lede: Nobody knows. This machine sweeps a tape of a few short words and rewrites them at every pass, and their order looks random. This page runs it in your browser.

facts.text: No halt in the C simulator; 22,985 cells visited.
No halt, proved in Lean; the first 10,000 by the kernel alone.
The growth shape of the two sides of the tape (see below).

sections.heading: Words at the two ends
html: At the left end the tape is mostly runs of the six-cell word 001011 and blocks like 000 10 11 0 11 0 11; at the right end it is stretches of 1 0 1 0 … separated by 0 0.
Two of the moves are simple erasures. C erases a block of 1s going right:
and D, with a 1 ahead, erases a block of 1s going left (Lean: erase_C, erase_D). The rest of each sweep is irregular zig-zag.

sections.heading: F must read a 1
html: Only F reading a 1 halts. F is entered from E reading a 1 and moving left:
F is rare: 111,044 visits in the first 2·108 steps, always on a 0.

sections.heading: The shape of the run
html: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.501). Right of the start it grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.476).
After 109 steps the tape spans 22,985 cells (15,283 left of the start, 1,695 right), with a density of 1s of 0.516.
These are measurements of one bounded run, sorted by tools/py/bbtools/triage.py; the macro structure behind them is the next thing to find.

sections.heading: Related machines
html: Other holdouts of the list of 608 that are tied to this one. The comparison of tables is exact; everything about runs was checked on the first 107 steps of each machine and is an observation, not a proof (holdouts/related.py, holdouts/related.json).

Same table as the machine below, started in another state. Renaming the states as shown turns this machine's table into the other one, the halting transition included. The other machine starts in its own state A, which is not this machine's A: its run from blank tape is the run of this table started in another state. These are different runs: in the first 107 steps of each, no configuration of this machine's run occurs in the other, even up to a shift of the tape. So each of these holdouts is its own halting question, and settling one does not settle another.

summary: Two-sided bouncer: runs of the 6-cell word 001011 and blocks 000 10 11 0 11 0 11 on the left, stretches of 1010… separated by 00 on the right; the mixture changes irregularly. Open.
